messages.subject: Guava in Renjin?
parts:
I´m implementing a Ruby Gem that integrates with MDArray.  This integration is falling and NetCDF-Java developers believe it might be a problem with Guava.  I´ve checked and it seens that Renjin actually uses Guava, is that so?  Is yes, what version does it use?

Thanks,


Rodrigo

messages.author: f06db63329fab1f9
messages.subject: Re: Guava in Renjin?
parts:
Renjin does use Guava; the latest snapshot uses version 17.0

There is an open ticket for repackaging guava and other commonly used libraries that are want to cause version conflicts:
https://github.com/bedatadriven/renjin/issues/63

I'm going to do a round of fixes next week and will try to get this one in as it's relatively straightforward.

Would love to see how you've approached the integration, do you have sample code anywhere?

Best,
Alex

Hi Bertram,

I´m getting ready to publish version 0.2.0 of SciCom.  This version will not yet have the integration with MDArray.  MDArray should follow shortly after, unless anyone finds anything really wrong with the initial version.  I´m quite pleasantly surprised with the level of integration that is possible between Ruby (SciCom) and Renjin.  Bellow some examples of R code and SciCom code... please let me know what you think.

This is an example of calculating the correlation matrix without using the build-in functions

R solution SciCom Solution
 
require 'scicon'
# Create a matrix and give it rownames and colnames
# Create a matrix and give it rownames and colnames
set.seed(42)
R.set__seed(42)
Xij <- matrix(sample(seq(0, 9), 40, replace = TRUE), ncol = 4) xij = R.matrix(R.sample(R.seq(0, 9), 40, replace: TRUE), ncol: 4)
rownames(Xij) <- paste("S", seq(1, dim(Xij)[1]), sep = "")
 xij.fassign(:rownames, R.paste("S", R.seq(1, xij.attr.dim[1]), sep: ""))
colnames(Xij) <- paste("V", seq(1, dim(Xij)[2]), sep = "") xij.fassign(:colnames, R.paste("V", R.seq(1, xij.attr.dim[2]), sep: ""))
   
# find the means of the columns
 # find the means of the columns
n <- dim(Xij)[1]
 n = xij.dim[1]
one <- rep(1, n)
 one = R.rep(1, n)
X.means <- t(one) %*% Xij/n
 x_means = one.t._ :*, xij/n
   
# find the covariance of the matrix
 # find the covariance of the matrix
X.diff <- Xij - one %*% X.means
 x_diff = xij - (one._ :*, x_means)
X.cov <- t(X.diff) %*% X.diff/(n - 1)
 x_cov = (x_diff.t._ :*, x_diff/(n - 1)).round(2)
round(X.cov, 2)  
   
# find the correlation 
 # find the correlation 
sdi <- diag(1/sqrt(diag(X.cov)))
 sdi = (1 / x_cov.diag.sqrt).diag.round(2)
rownames(sdi) <- colnames(sdi) <- colnames(X.cov) sdi.fassign(:rownames, x_cov.rownames)
round(sdi, 2) sdi.fassign(:colnames, x_cov.colnames)
X.cor <- sdi %*% X.cov %*% sdi
 x_cor = ((sdi._ :*, x_cov)._ :*, sdi).round(2)
rownames(X.cor) <- colnames(X.cor) <- colnames(X.cov) x_cor.fassign(:rownames, x_cov.rownames)
round(X.cor, 2) x_cor.fassign(:colnames, x_cov.colnames)



Another example to print the number of days in every month of 2005:

require 'scicom'

everyday = R.seq(from: R.as__Date('2005-1-1'), to: R.as__Date('2005-12-31'), by: 'day')
cmonth = everyday.format('%b')
cmonth
  .factor(levels: cmonth.unique, ordered: TRUE)
  .table
  .pp

> [1] 31 28 31 30 31 30 31 31 30 31 30 31


So, how does that look?


Thanks

messages.author: f06db63329fab1f9
messages.subject: Re: Guava in Renjin?
parts:
Wow! That's quite cool.

Are you writing wrappers like R.rep by hand or is it possible to write some of sort of dynamic dispatch in Ruby that passes calls off to Renjin?

I took a look at your MDDoubleVector class - Very nice work but a bit unfortunate how much math is needed to get the index. Do you have an indication of the performance hit incurred when invoking one of Renjin's matrix operations on a matrix stored in MDArray? I fear that calling any of the methods from lapack or blas will bomb as Renjin will have to copy the matrix to column-major order as those routines are specifically coded against a column-major layout. 

This touches on a few ideas:
  • We could add a getMatrixElement(row, column) method that can be used by R primitives that explicitly operate on matrices, which would allow you to provide a more efficient accessor for objects using alternate layouts. This wouldn't be of much help with lapack/blas routines as they are coded and optimized against a column-major layout.
  • Renjin could also provide a mechanism by which the storage implementation can influence the choice of algorithm implementation. So if a user calls det(x) and x is a NetCDF matrix, we could invoke NetCDF's implementation instead of the "default" provided by netlib. 
Hannes is working on something similar with Renjin and MonetDB where we want to ship certain calls, or even sequences of calls, to MonetDB when the R object is actually referencing data in a MonetDB table/query.

Can I ask what kind of domain you're using scicom and the NetCDF integration with?

All the best,
Alex

messages.author: da2d889d1cc5c83c
messages.subject: Renjin and SciCom (was: Re: Guava in Renjin?)
parts: Bertram...

Em segunda-feira, 17 de novembro de 2014 21h08min54s UTC-2, Alexander Bertram escreveu:
Wow! That's quite cool.

Are you writing wrappers like R.rep by hand or is it possible to write some of sort of dynamic dispatch in Ruby that passes calls off to Renjin?

Almost everything is dynamically dispatched to Renjin.  The magic is basically done by method 'method_missing'.  I´ll describe a bit how the whole thing works so that you can help me identify potential problems and maybe think of ways of improving either SciCom or Renjin for better integration.

Lets begin with a simple example:

vec = R.c(1, 2.45, 3)

Ruby will try to find method 'c' on R class, since there is no such method, Ruby calls 'method_missing' passing the argument list to it.  'method_missing' calls 'parse' to parse the arguments.  In this case, every argument is an Numeric and 'parse' will basically convert the argument list to a string: "(1, 2.45, 3)".  'method_missing' then makes the following call:

# R.eval(" <method_name> + <arguments> "), which in this case is: 

R.eval("c(1, 2.45, 3)")  giving us the desired result.

Now lets do:

vec2 = R.c(vec, 4, 5)

Again, 'method_missing' is called, which calls 'parse'.  The first argument to parse is now a Ruby::Vector and parse does the following:

# create a temporary variable, lets call it sc_1234
# let vec.sexp be the actual java sexp for this vector, then:

R.eval("sc_1234 = vec.sexp")  # this stores the java vector in the sc_1234 variable

# finally return all parameters as a string: "(sc_1234, 4, 5)"
# Now let Renjin do the work:

R.eval("c(sc_1234, 4, 5)")

# return of the above is the vector [1, 2.5, 3, 4, 5] as expected
# finally, we remove the temporary variable sc_1234, from Renjin name space in the hope that this will allow gc to work.  

Every statement in SciCom is converted to an evaluable string that can be passed to Renjin 'eval'.  Now, this adds some overhead, but unless we put a SciCom statment inside a large loop this should be reasonable.  One way that integration could be improved is if there was some way of calling 'eval' on a SEXP and not on a string.  Maybe you have this already, but I couldn´t find a way of doing it.

Now, if we have

vec.mean

Then again we call 'method_missing' of the Vector class.  In this case, first we check if 'mean' is a named element of the vector.  If it is, then we call:

R.eval("vec[mean]")

If mean is not a named element of the vector, then we call:

R.eval("mean(vec)")

Which calculates the mean of the vector.  Again, this is just translating Ruby statements onto R evaluable strings.

Some new methods had to be defined.  For instance we have method '_' in order to simulate methods such as %in%.  So here we do

vec._ :in, vec2

This is a call to the '_' method with 2 arguments ':in' and 'vec2'.  This translates to the correct R call:

R.eval("vec %in% vec2")

In place of ':in' we can put any other string.

Methods and variable that have a '.' on their names are used in SciCom with '__' notation.  So, read.csv in R is written as read__csv.  'method_missing' converts '__' to '.' before calling eval.  So, if there is any variable in R written with '__' there will be no way to access it, other than calling R.eval directly.

'method_missing' is really the great magic!

I took a look at your MDDoubleVector class - Very nice work but a bit unfortunate how much math is needed to get the index. Do you have an indication of the performance hit incurred when invoking one of Renjin's matrix operations on a matrix stored in MDArray? I fear that calling any of the methods from lapack or blas will bomb as Renjin will have to copy the matrix to column-major order as those routines are specifically coded against a column-major layout.

If I understand correctly Renjin´s code, then there isn´t really any copying, just index calculation.  When Renjin wants an array element it will call getElementAsDouble passing the element index in column-major order.  SciCom takes this value and translates it to the proper value in row-major order.  There is some complexity on the calculation, mainly because R semantics for multi-dimensions are different than MDArrays semantics, but it shouldn´t have all this impact.  However, I have not yet benchmarked it.  I´ll be doing this for the next version of SciCom.

This touches on a few ideas:
  • We could add a getMatrixElement(row, column) method that can be used by R primitives that explicitly operate on matrices, which would allow you to provide a more efficient accessor for objects using alternate layouts. This wouldn't be of much help with lapack/blas routines as they are coded and optimized against a column-major layout.

Hummmm... really, I don´t know how lapack/blas will work (or not) with this implementation.  Those routines don´t call getElementAsDouble?  If so, then SciCom will actually return a wrong value as the data is in row-major order and lapack/blas will read it as column-major: big problem! Is that so?

• Renjin could also provide a mechanism by which the storage implementation can influence the choice of algorithm implementation. So if a user calls det(x) and x is a NetCDF matrix, we could invoke NetCDF's implementation instead of the "default" provided by netlib.

This could be good, but I would have to make sure that every R method that works on matrices has an equivalent in SciCom/MDArray.  Actually, matrix algebra is not done by NetCDF matrix, but by ParallelColt.  MDArray provides MDMatrix class which converts a NetCDF Array onto a ParallelColt matrix.

Both NetCDF and ParallelColt arrays have a one dimensional Java Array as their backing store, so there is no need to any data copying.

Maybe we could work the other way around and I could use a standard backing store provided by Renjin.  I use ParallelColt because I read that it was one of the fastest and more robust libraries for Java matrix algebra, but I have no special "love" for it.  Actually ParallelColt is an old library and not maintained anymore which is unfortunate.  Works fine, though.  On the other hand, NetCDF Array is well maintained and is the base for a lot of nice functionality such as writing netcdf files, and the GRIB server, which if I understand correctly allows the distribution of large datasets through the web.

So, would it be possible for Renjin to extract its Java Matrix/Array library so that it could be used by other applications?  Does that make sense?  Or could you use something like CommonMath or even ParallelColt (and give it a face lift)?  I think its pretty bad that there are lots of projects doing basically the same thing.

Hannes is working on something similar with Renjin and MonetDB where we want to ship certain calls, or even sequences of calls, to MonetDB when the R object is actually referencing data in a MonetDB table/query.
I´m sure that this glue can be provided by Ruby.
What kind of domain are you using the Ruby->Renjin->NetCDF integration with? I'd be super interested to see how it scales.

I´m actually in information security and I believe that the future of this field will be by using predictive analytics.  There is no other way to go through millions of security events every day and hope to see something if not by using analytics.  If you have some interest in this field, you could take a look at: "Data-Driven Security".  At this moment though, I haven´t yet used the integration in production.  

We are still missing a good graphics library to integrate with all the rest.  I´m hoping that this might be provided by the Ruby community.  There are some new libraries such as NyaPlot and daru that I hope will integrate with SciCom/MDArray.

Thanks for Renjin.... great library.... Cheers!!


Rodrigo
